section.title: Instructions on Prayer and Worship
section.sectionRationale: Paul turns from doctrine to the gathered church at prayer. First of all, prayer is to be made for everyone, including rulers, grounded in the truth that there is one God and one mediator who gave Himself a ransom for all. He then directs the conduct of men and women in worship, ending with the much debated instruction about women, teaching, and authority.
section.thesis: Because God desires all kinds of people to be saved through the one mediator, Christ Jesus, the church at worship is to pray for everyone, and men and women alike are to conduct themselves in godliness, reverence, and good works.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the call to pray for all people grounded in the one God and one mediator; the conduct of men and women in worship; and the debated instruction on a woman learning quietly, named fairly with its strongest orthodox readings.

verses.text: First of all, then, I urge that petitions, prayers, {{enteuxis|intercessions}}, and thanksgiving be offered for everyone,
for kings and all those in authority, so that we may lead tranquil and quiet lives in all {{eusebeia|godliness}} and dignity.
This is good and pleasing in the sight of God our Savior,
who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.
For there is one God, and there is one {{mesites|mediator}} between God and men, the man Christ Jesus,
who gave Himself as a {{antilytron|ransom}} for all, the testimony that was given at just the right time.
For this reason I was appointed as a preacher, an apostle, and a faithful and true teacher of the Gentiles. I am telling the truth; I am not lying about anything.
Therefore I want the men everywhere to pray, lifting up holy hands, without anger or dissension.
Likewise, I want the women to adorn themselves with respectable apparel, with modesty, and with self-control, not with braided hair or gold or pearls or expensive clothes,
but with good deeds, as is proper for women who profess to worship God.

units.label: A woman learning, and the debate

verses.text: A woman must learn in {{hesychia|quietness}} and full submissiveness.
I do not permit a woman to teach or to {{authenteo|exercise authority}} over a man; she is to remain quiet.
For Adam was formed first, and then Eve.
And it was not Adam who was deceived, but the woman who was deceived and fell into transgression.
Women, however, will be saved through childbearing, if they continue in faith, love, and holiness, with {{sophrosyne|self-control}}.

enteuxis.gloss: Intercession, a petition or approach made on behalf of another, even an appeal to a king. It is one of four words Paul heaps up for prayer, stressing that the church is to bring the needs of all people, especially outsiders and rulers, before God.

eusebeia.gloss: Godliness, true reverence for God worked out in daily life. It is a key word of the Pastoral Epistles, describing a life that honors God. Peaceful public order is desired so believers may live out this godliness undisturbed.

mesites.gloss: A mediator, one who stands between two parties to bring them together. Paul insists there is only one between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. He alone bridges the gap, being truly God and truly man, which is why prayer and salvation come through Him alone.

antilytron.gloss: A ransom, the price paid to release a captive, with the prefix anti stressing a substitute given in exchange. Christ gave Himself as this ransom for all, His life laid down in place of sinners to set them free.

hesychia.gloss: Quietness, stillness, a settled and peaceable spirit rather than mere silence. The same word describes the tranquil life all believers are to seek in verse 2. A woman is to learn in this quietness, that is, in a teachable, unclamorous manner.

authenteo.gloss: To exercise authority over, a rare word appearing only here in the New Testament. Its precise nuance is debated, ranging from a neutral holding of authority to a domineering or self-assumed control. Its rarity is one reason this passage is discussed so carefully.

sophrosyne.gloss: Self-control, soundness of mind, sober good sense. It frames the whole instruction to women, appearing in verse 9 and again in verse 15. This inner self-mastery, not outward display, marks the woman who professes to worship God.

basic.context: Paul says the first priority in worship is prayer, offered for everyone, including kings and rulers, so the church can live peaceful, godly lives. This pleases God, who wants all kinds of people saved. The reason is the gospel: one God, one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave Himself a ransom for all. Paul then directs how men and women should conduct themselves in worship, ending with a debated instruction about women learning quietly.
basic.hermeneutics: The call to prayer and the gospel ground beneath it are plainly for all time. The instruction on women, teaching, and authority is read differently by faithful Christians; the study names the main orthodox readings without pretending the debate does not exist. Whatever one's view, the passage upholds the full worth of women and their call to learn.
basic.originalLanguages: Prayer includes enteuxis, intercession, so believers may live in eusebeia, godliness. There is one mesites, mediator, Christ, who gave Himself an antilytron, ransom. A woman is to learn in hesychia, quietness, and the debated word authenteo, exercise authority, appears only here, framed by sophrosyne, self-control.
basic.typology: The one mediator fulfills the whole priestly system: where priests once stood between God and Israel, Christ is the final and perfect mediator. His ransom fulfills every offering that pointed to a life given in place of sinners.
basic.christ: The center is verses 5 and 6: one God, one mediator, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself a ransom for all. Salvation, prayer, and access to God all run through Him alone. He is both the ground of our praying and the content of the truth all are to come to know.
basic.god: God is our Savior who wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth. He is one, and He is pleased when His people pray for all, including those in authority. His saving desire reaches beyond Israel to the nations, which is why Paul was made a teacher of the Gentiles.
basic.crossReferences: Mark 10 says the Son of Man came to give His life a ransom for many. Hebrews 9 presents Christ as the mediator of a new covenant. Genesis 2 and 3 stand behind Paul's appeal to creation and the fall.
basic.oneStory: God has always meant to gather a people from every nation to Himself. Here the church prays for all people because the one mediator gave Himself a ransom for all, and worship is ordered so that the household of God displays godliness. It is part of God's long work of reconciling the world to Himself through His Son.

context.literary:
The chapter's first seven verses are held together by a single small word. 'Everyone' in verse 1, 'all those in authority' in verse 2, 'all godliness' in the same verse, 'everyone to be saved' in verse 4 and 'a ransom for all' in verse 6 are all forms of the Greek pas. The paragraph is built to say, again and again, that the church's horizon is as wide as God's. Verse 8 then adds 'the men everywhere,' so the same universality reaches into every place where the church gathers.

The second half is organised around Paul's own wants. 'I want the men... to pray' in verse 8 and 'likewise, I want the women' in verse 9 share one verb, since the second sentence borrows its 'I want' from the first. Verse 12 switches to a different construction, 'I do not permit,' and verses 13 and 14 give reasons introduced by 'for.' The unit therefore moves from a wish to a ruling to a justification.

Two motifs frame the chapter. The first is quietness. Verse 2 hopes for 'tranquil and quiet lives,' and verses 11 and 12 use the same word family for the woman's learning and silence. The church is meant to be quiet outwardly so that the gospel can be heard. The second is self-control, which stands at verse 9 and again at the very end in verse 15, so the whole unit about women is wrapped in that virtue.

Verse 15 is the most compressed sentence in the chapter, with a shift from singular to plural subject, 'a woman... they,' and a condition about continuing. Much of the debate about the chapter comes from the way the Greek moves in these final lines, so readers should keep the whole movement in view, prayer for the world, the one mediator, and then the conduct of the gathered people, rather than lifting verse 12 out as a stand-alone rule.
context.historical:
Paul asks the church to pray for kings and all in authority at a time when Christians were a small and easily suspected minority. Rulers could be hostile, and Paul does not pretend otherwise. His instruction continues a long Jewish habit of prayer for a pagan ruler. Jeremiah told the exiles in Babylon, 'Seek the prosperity of the city... Pray to the LORD on its behalf,' Jeremiah 29:7, and the Persian king asked that sacrifices be offered 'to pray for the lives of the king and his sons,' Ezra 6:10. The stated purpose is practical: 'tranquil and quiet lives' in which the gospel can be lived and heard.

The posture in verse 8 is a familiar one. Solomon prayed with his hands spread toward heaven, 1 Kings 8:22, and the psalmist asked that his 'uplifted hands' be like the evening offering, Psalm 141:2. Hands raised in worship needed to be 'holy,' because Isaiah 1:15 warned that hands full of blood make prayer useless. Paul's remark about 'anger or dissension' implies that arguments over the false teaching had spilled into the gathering.

The instruction about adornment fits the wealth of Ephesus. Braided and elaborately arranged hair, gold and pearls marked rank and money, and Paul wants worship to be a place where such display does not set believers against one another. Isaiah had earlier criticised the finery of proud women in Jerusalem, Isaiah 3:16 to 24, and Peter gives a similar warning, 1 Peter 3:3 and 4.

The instruction on teaching and authority must be read with what the letters say about the false teachers. Some of them worked their way into households, 2 Timothy 3:6 and 7, and younger widows were being drawn into idleness and gossip, 1 Timothy 5:13 to 15. It is also notable that Paul commands a woman to learn at all. Mary sat 'at the Lord's feet' in the position of a disciple, Luke 10:39, and the same openness to women learning is assumed here.
context.canonical:
Paul's appeal to Genesis in verses 13 and 14 ties this paragraph to the first three chapters of the Bible. He reads Genesis 2:7 and 2:18 to 22 as an account of order, the man formed first, and Genesis 3:13 as an account of deception. 2 Corinthians 11:3 uses the same event as a warning for the whole church: 'just as Eve was deceived by the serpent's cunning.' Romans 5:14 calls Adam 'a pattern of the One to come.'

On men and women in worship, the passage belongs with 1 Corinthians 11:3 to 16, where women pray and prophesy in the assembly, and 1 Corinthians 14:34 and 35, which asks women to be silent in a context of weighing prophecy. Titus 2:3 to 5 gives older women a teaching role among younger women. Elsewhere women are named as fellow workers, such as Priscilla, who helped explain 'the way of God more accurately' to Apollos, Acts 18:26, and Phoebe, a servant of the church in Cenchrea, Romans 16:1. Galatians 3:28 says that in Christ there is 'neither... male nor female,' and any adequate reading has to account for all these texts together.

The centre of the chapter belongs to the wider biblical teaching of one God and one mediator. 'The LORD our God, the LORD is One,' Deuteronomy 6:4, becomes in Paul's creed, 'there is but one God, the Father... and there is but one Lord, Jesus Christ,' 1 Corinthians 8:6. Hebrews develops the idea of Christ as mediator in 8:6, 9:15 and 12:24, and Jesus himself said he came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The call to pray for all echoes Ezekiel 18:23, 2 Peter 3:9 and Titus 2:11, which also speak of God's desire for the salvation of everyone.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul meant this chapter to reset what a church thinks it is for. Before he says anything about who does what in worship, he says that the church's first work is prayer, and that this prayer reaches everyone, including the rulers who might be its enemies. A congregation that has become inward and quarrelsome is told to look outward, because God does.

He also wanted to anchor that outward look in the gospel itself. The 'for' of verse 5 gives the reason: there is one God and one mediator, so there is no one for whom the door is closed in principle and no one who can reach God by another way. The testimony given 'at just the right time' makes the church's prayer a response to an event, not wishful thinking.

The second half of the chapter is addressed to a church in a particular crisis. Men are to leave off anger and quarrelling when they pray, and women are to put goodness before display. Paul wanted worship to look like the gospel it proclaims, peaceable, modest and ready for good works.

In verses 11 to 15 he gives an instruction about a woman's learning and teaching, based on creation and the fall. What he intended his first readers to do is clear in its direction, even if its exact scope is argued: women are to learn, and the church is not to let teaching fall under the influence of the false teachers who had found a hearing among some of them. The reasons he gives point to something beyond local custom, and readers have disagreed about how far beyond. It would be dishonest to say the passage settles every question about the roles of women in the church today, and equally dishonest to say it says nothing.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
Some of the chapter is straightforward command that applies everywhere. Believers are to pray for everyone, give thanks for them and pray for those in authority. The central confession of one mediator is a statement of truth, not a local custom. These parts are prescriptive for the church at all times.

Some details are descriptions of how the commands were carried out in the first century. Lifting holy hands is one of several postures for prayer found in Scripture, and the apostle's concern is that the hands be holy, not that the position be the same in every church. The prohibition on braided hair, gold and pearls aims at ostentation and at wealth that divides the church. Most readers across the traditions treat the principle, modesty, good works and no showing off, as binding and the particular items as examples of the culture's status symbols.

The instruction in verses 11 to 15 is the hardest part. Faithful Christians who hold the Bible to be God's word read it differently. Some consider the reasons Paul gives, creation order and the deception of Eve, to make the restriction on teaching and exercising authority over men a standing principle for the church's public teaching. Others believe the instruction answers a specific situation of false teaching in Ephesus and that its underlying principle is that the church must not be led by untested or unqualified teachers. Both agree that women are to be taught, that they are full participants in the church's prayer and good works, and that no one should use the passage to demean women. The honest approach is to hold the reading one has reached with humility toward those who differ.

debates.question: Does verse 12 set a permanent limit on women teaching and holding authority over men in the church?

views.label: A permanent limit grounded in creation
views.case: Paul bases the instruction on creation, 'Adam was formed first,' not on a passing custom. Because the reasons come from Genesis, not Ephesus, the instruction is read as binding in every church. On this view, 3:1 to 7 on overseers, and Paul's pattern of appointing men as elders, fit with the same principle, while women are fully free to teach other women and children, Titus 2:3 to 5, and to serve in many ways.

views.label: A response to the Ephesian situation
views.case: Others argue that Paul addresses a place where false teachers had influenced women, 2 Timothy 3:6 and 7, 1 Timothy 5:13, and that the present tense 'I do not permit' reflects a particular situation. They add that Paul works with women as teachers and leaders elsewhere, Romans 16:1 to 7, Acts 18:26, and that the appeal to Genesis shows what Paul wants to correct, domineering or uninstructed teaching, rather than creating a rule about roles.

views.label: A restriction on authoritative public teaching of the church's doctrine
views.case: A middle view holds that Paul speaks about the office of authoritative teaching and governance that guards the apostolic deposit, as in verses 1:3 to 11 and 3:1 to 7. Women are free to teach and share in many ways, but the specific function of authoritative doctrinal oversight is reserved for qualified men.

debates.bearing: The three readings agree on far more than they dispute: women are to learn, the church guards sound teaching, and the creation texts matter. Where they differ is on whether verse 12 is a rule for all churches, so each reader should weigh the creation argument and the Ephesian context with care.

debates.question: What does 'exercise authority' mean in verse 12?

views.label: To hold authority in the ordinary sense
views.case: The verb authenteo occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, so its sense is argued from other Greek writing. Some scholars conclude that it carries the ordinary sense of exercising authority, and that Paul forbids a woman to do this over a man.

views.label: To domineer or usurp
views.case: Others hold that in the period the word could carry a negative sense, to dominate or take over, and that Paul forbids a domineering attitude, not legitimate authority.

views.label: To act on one's own authority or to originate
views.case: A third group suggests a sense close to acting independently of the recognised leadership. The word's rarity makes certainty impossible.

debates.bearing: The meaning of one rare word cannot carry the whole question, so interpreters weigh it together with the creation argument. Because the dispute is real, no reading should be presented as the only one the text allows.

debates.question: Does God want 'everyone' to be saved in verse 4?

views.label: Every individual
views.case: Paul says 'everyone' in verse 1 and 'a ransom for all' in verse 6, and 2 Peter 3:9 speaks of God not wanting anyone to perish. Read this way, God's revealed desire is for every person and his offer is genuine.

views.label: All kinds of people
views.case: Others note that the context of kings and authorities, Jew and Gentile, suggests classes of people, and that the same passage reads, 'a teacher of the Gentiles,' verse 7. On this reading Paul is saying that no group is excluded, and the language describes who is included, not that every individual will be.

views.label: God's desire and God's decree distinguished
views.case: Others hold that Scripture distinguishes what God commands and desires from what he decrees, as in Ezekiel 18:23, where he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. His desire for repentance is real even though not all repent.

debates.bearing: All three agree that the church's prayer and preaching are to be offered to everyone without exception, and that salvation comes only through the one mediator.

debates.question: What does 'saved through childbearing' mean in verse 15?

views.label: Through the birth of the Messiah
views.case: The Greek has 'the childbearing,' with the article, which some read as the birth of Christ through whom salvation comes, answering Genesis 3:15 and Galatians 4:4. Against this, the verse goes on to a condition of continuing in faith.

views.label: Preserved safely through childbirth
views.case: Some think Paul promises that a woman will be brought safely through childbirth, the particular pain of the curse in Genesis 3:16, if she lives in faith. The difficulty is that believing women have died in childbirth.

views.label: Saved while living out her calling
views.case: Another reading takes 'saved' in the ordinary sense and 'childbearing' as shorthand for a woman's domestic role. Salvation is not earned by it, but those who are saved walk in it, together with faith, love and holiness, 1 Timothy 5:14.

debates.bearing: No reading can mean that a woman earns salvation by having children, which would contradict verses 5 and 6. The verse closes the paragraph by pointing to faith, love and holiness as the shape of a saved life.

study.originalLanguages:
The opening gathers four words for prayer. Petition, deesis, is the cry of need. Prayer, proseuche, is the general word for speaking to God. Intercession names a bold approach on behalf of others. Thanksgiving, eucharistia, is the offering of gratitude. Paul wants all four offered for everyone, including those in authority, so the list includes a call to be thankful for people who may not be friends.

The goal of verse 4 is 'the knowledge of the truth,' epignosis aletheias, a full or accurate knowledge. The same phrase appears in 2 Timothy 2:25, 2 Timothy 3:7 and Titus 1:1, and it is an expression Paul uses for coming to know the gospel. In 2 Timothy 3:7 he speaks of people 'always learning but never able to come to a knowledge of the truth,' which is exactly the opposite of what God wants for the people of this passage.

In verse 5 the mediator is 'the man Christ Jesus.' The Greek word is anthropos, a human being, and it is deliberately chosen. The one who stands between God and people has to be on both sides, and so the verse names his humanity at the very point it speaks of his work. The phrase 'at just the right time' in verse 6 is literally 'in its own times,' kairois idiois, the plural of seasons God has appointed. Paul uses a similar idea in Galatians 4:4, 'when the time had fully come.'

The word 'submissiveness' in verse 11 is hypotage, the noun for orderly subordination, as when an army is arranged under a commander. It occurs elsewhere in Paul in 1 Timothy 3:4, where an overseer must keep his children 'under control,' and in 2 Corinthians 9:13 and Galatians 2:5. The context decides whether the submission is to God's word, to teachers, to husband or to the order of the assembly, and the translation 'full submissiveness' leaves that open.

In verse 14 the woman was 'deceived,' exapatao, a strengthened form of the verb to deceive, the same compound Paul uses of Eve in 2 Corinthians 11:3. The man by contrast did not fall by deception but 'transgression,' a related word, parabasis, which means stepping across a line. Paul uses that word for Adam in Romans 5:14, 'the way that Adam transgressed.'

The verb 'saved' in verse 15 is sozo, which in the New Testament usually means rescued in the full sense of salvation but can speak of physical deliverance. That range is one reason the verse is read in different ways.

typology.type: Moses and the priests as mediators, verse 5
typology.fulfillment: Israel needed someone to stand between God and the people. Moses said, 'I was standing between the LORD and you to declare to you the word of the LORD,' Deuteronomy 5:5, and Paul calls the law 'administered through angels by a mediator,' Galatians 3:19. The priests offered sacrifices day after day. The correspondence is real, but Christ exceeds it: he is 'the mediator of a new covenant,' Hebrews 9:15, whose ministry is 'much more excellent,' Hebrews 8:6, and who 'always lives to intercede,' Hebrews 7:25. The type falls short because Moses was a mediator of a covenant that could not remove sin, and the priests died; Christ is both man and God, and lives.

The law required a payment 'for his life' when Israel was numbered, Exodus 30:12, and spoke of redeeming what had been lost. Isaiah described a servant who would bear 'the sin of many' and 'make intercession for the transgressors,' Isaiah 53:12. Jesus took that pattern when he said he came 'to give His life as a ransom for many,' Mark 10:45. The correspondence is substitution, a life given for lives. The escalation is that Christ gives himself, not an animal or a coin, and Titus 2:14 says he 'gave Himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness.' The Old Testament payments were temporary; his ransom is final.

The psalmist asks that his prayer be 'set before You like incense, my uplifted hands like the evening offering,' Psalm 141:2, treating prayer as a priestly offering. Revelation 8:3 and 4 shows the prayers of the saints rising with the incense before God's throne. In Christ, access is not limited to a priestly class: 'through Him we both have access to the Father by one Spirit,' Ephesians 2:18, and believers are a 'royal priesthood,' 1 Peter 2:9. The picture falls short if it suggests that our prayers are acceptable on their own merit, since they rise through the mediator of verse 5.

typology.type: The woman and her offspring, verses 13 to 15
typology.fulfillment: Paul reaches back to Genesis 2 and 3, where the woman was deceived and her pain in childbearing was named, Genesis 3:13 and 16, and where a promise was spoken about her offspring who would crush the serpent's head, Genesis 3:15. If verse 15 recalls that promise, it points to Christ, 'born of a woman,' Galatians 4:4. Adam is also a pattern of the One to come, Romans 5:14, and Christ is the last Adam, 1 Corinthians 15:45. These links are suggested rather than stated outright in this passage, and the type falls short because ordinary motherhood is not itself saving.

study.christ:
The two verses at the centre of the chapter are among the shortest and fullest statements of Christ's work anywhere in the letters. 'There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave Himself as a ransom for all.' Each phrase is worth reading slowly.

The sentence begins with 'one.' A mediator is needed when two parties are apart, and Galatians 3:20 reminds us that 'a mediator is unnecessary... for only one party; but God is one.' In the Old Testament, Moses stood between God and the people, and priests stood between them again with their sacrifices. Paul says that this has now been done in one person, once. The oneness of God, which Israel confessed in Deuteronomy 6:4, has a counterpart in the oneness of the mediator, so that salvation is not left to a shifting group of intermediaries. 1 Corinthians 8:6 says the same: one God, the Father, and one Lord, Jesus Christ.

The mediator is 'the man.' Paul does not say he was God only, nor that he only looked like a man. His humanity is what makes him fit to stand for us, and the writer of Hebrews teaches the same thing, that Jesus shared our flesh and blood so that he could be a faithful high priest. His divinity is what makes him able to bear what we cannot, and 1 Timothy 3:16 will say that God was manifested in the flesh. The phrase says that the one who reaches across the gap is both ends of it.

He 'gave Himself.' The ransom is not money or an animal but himself. Mark 10:45 shows that the Lord described his own mission in these terms, and Isaiah 53:10 to 12 foretold the servant who would bear the sin of many. Ephesians 5:25 and Titus 2:14 use the same words about Christ's self-giving, 'gave Himself up for her' and 'gave Himself for us.' The scope is 'all,' which means the offer is universal and no group is shut out.

Hebrews 7:25 completes the picture by saying that he 'always lives to intercede for them.' The mediator did not leave his work at the cross; he continues in it. That is why Paul can call the church to pray for everyone, since prayer rises through him, Hebrews 4:16.

Even the section on women shows something of Christ. In Luke 10:39 Jesus welcomed Mary as a learner at his feet, and in John 20:17 and 18 he sent Mary Magdalene as the first messenger of his resurrection. These accounts keep the chapter's pastoral conversation about women in the light of his own example.

A caution applies. The mediator is not a hidden figure in every detail of the chapter. The links rest on the explicit confession of verses 5 and 6 and on the New Testament passages that explain them.
study.god:
The God of this chapter is introduced by a title that sets the tone: 'God our Savior.' He is the Savior before he is the Lawgiver, and in verse 4 we learn his heart: he 'wants everyone to be saved and to come to the knowledge of the truth.' That sentence should be allowed to stand in its full warmth. The God of Scripture does not take pleasure in the death of the wicked, Ezekiel 18:23, and is 'patient with you, not wanting anyone to perish,' 2 Peter 3:9. The same Scripture also teaches that not everyone is saved, and Christians have long wrestled with how to hold both together, as the debates above record. What the verse insists on is that the church can never speak of God as grudging, and that its prayers and its preaching are never to be narrowed to a chosen few.

He is one, as Israel confessed, and the oneness has consequences. There is no rival god to whom a person might turn, no second route, and no human intermediary who can stand in for the mediator he himself provided. God is the one who devised the way back and who provided the price. The ransom is not extracted from a reluctant Father by a kindly Son. The Father is 'God our Savior,' and the Son 'gave Himself' with the Father's will, Isaiah 53:10.

He rules over history and its timing. The testimony was given 'at just the right time,' in its proper seasons, and rulers hold power under his sovereignty. Romans 13:1 says that 'there is no authority except that which is from God,' and Acts 17:26 says he 'determined their appointed times.' So prayer for kings is not a recognition of their divinity, but an appeal to the God who sits above them.

He cares about the way his people worship. He asks for holy hands, a peaceable spirit, modest dress and good works. These are not trivial. The God who is rich in mercy wants a people whose worship matches what they confess.

He values the learning of both men and women. The command that a woman learn is given in a world that often neglected it, and the God who made man and woman in his image sees both as capable of knowing the truth.

For worship, the chapter shapes the tone of our prayers. They begin with thanksgiving, reach outward to the people we would rather ignore, and rest on the mediator rather than on the quality of our voices.

crossReferences.note: The exiles in Babylon are told to seek the city's prosperity and pray to the LORD for it. This is the Old Testament pattern behind Paul's call to pray for kings, and it shows that praying for hostile or foreign rulers was an ancient practice of God's people.

God asks whether he takes pleasure in the death of the wicked and says he would rather that they turn from their ways and live. It supports the claim of verse 4 that God wants everyone to be saved, and it shows that this desire is old.

The Shema confesses that the LORD is one. Verse 5 of 1 Timothy 2 begins from the same confession, 'there is one God,' and then adds one mediator, so that Israel's central creed is carried into the gospel.
The law was given through a mediator, and 'God is one.' The passage helps explain why Paul stresses oneness: a mediator implies two parties, and Christ is the one who stands between God and people.

Jesus says he came 'to give His life as a ransom for many.' It is the source of the ransom language in verse 6, and it shows that Paul is passing on the Lord's own account of his death rather than inventing a new theory.
The covenant that Jesus mediates is better and rests on better promises. It develops the title 'mediator' from verse 5 and shows how it improves on the work of Moses and the priests.

The psalmist asks that his prayer be like incense and his uplifted hands like the evening offering. It shows that lifting hands was a recognised posture of prayer and that prayer was understood as an offering.

The account of the woman's creation from the man, which stands behind Paul's remark that Adam was formed first. Reading it carefully shows that the woman is also described as 'a suitable helper,' so Paul's appeal has to be heard together with the dignity this text gives her.

Paul fears that the Corinthians will be led astray as Eve was deceived by the serpent's cunning. It shows that he uses Eve's deception as a warning against false teaching for the whole church, which helps interpret verse 14.

Older women are to be teachers of what is good and to train the younger women. It shows that Paul expected women to teach, in a particular setting, and it must be taken into account with 1 Timothy 2:12.

Peter warns against outward adornment such as braided hair, gold jewellery and fine clothes, and commends a gentle and quiet spirit. The parallel confirms that Paul's concern is display, not beauty, and that the principle was held across the apostles.
Adam is called 'a pattern of the One to come.' It connects the first man, whom Paul mentions in verse 13, to Christ, so the creation reference in the chapter opens onto the theme of the one mediator.

study.oneStory:
The first chapters of Genesis describe a world made for a man and a woman in God's image, then broken by deception and disobedience. The rest of the Bible is God's work to bring people back, and 1 Timothy 2 takes up several strands of that story at once. Paul reaches back to Adam and Eve in verses 13 and 14 because the church still lives within what they began, and he reaches forward in verses 5 and 6 to the one who undoes it.

The call to pray for everyone belongs to the promise made to Abraham, that all the families of the earth would be blessed. For most of Israel's history the promise was carried by one nation, and the nations were mostly outsiders. Paul describes himself in verse 7 as 'a teacher of the Gentiles,' which says that the promise has now burst its old boundaries. When Paul tells the church to pray for kings and for everyone, he is describing a people who have begun to live as the blessing meant for the whole earth.

The one mediator answers the longing built into the Old Testament. Moses stood between God and the people, priests offered sacrifice again and again, and the prophets spoke of a servant who would bear the sin of many. Paul says that all of that has reached its goal. The ransom has been paid once, at the right time, and what remains is to proclaim it.

The portion on men and women belongs to the story of a creation order that sin damaged and that redemption is restoring. The tension in Genesis 3:16 between the woman and the man is not the end of the story; Galatians 3:28 says that in Christ the barriers are broken down, and the church now has to live in the overlap between the old world's damage and the new world's healing. Reasonable believers differ over what that looks like in the assembly, and that is itself a sign of how seriously they take both creation and redemption.

The story ends with a multitude 'from every nation and tribe and people and tongue,' Revelation 7:9, and with kings bringing their glory into the city, Revelation 21:24. Paul's call to pray for rulers and to want the salvation of all is a rehearsal of that ending, an early sign of the day when God's desire has been fulfilled and the ransomed from every place stand before the Lamb.

quiz.q: What does Paul say should be the first priority in the church's worship?

options.text: Prayer, including intercession and thanksgiving, offered for everyone.
options.note: Verses 1 and 2 urge prayer for all people, including rulers.

options.text: Collecting an offering before anything else.
options.note: Giving matters elsewhere, but Paul names prayer for all as first of all here.

options.text: Debating the false teachers publicly.
options.note: The priority is prayer, not public dispute.

options.text: Praying only for fellow believers.
options.note: Paul explicitly widens prayer to everyone, including kings.

quiz.q: On what gospel truth does Paul ground the call to pray for all?

options.text: There is one God and one mediator, Christ Jesus, who gave Himself a ransom for all.
options.note: Verses 5 and 6 supply the reason for praying for everyone.

options.text: That every religion leads to the same God.
options.note: Paul insists on one mediator, not many roads; this misreads him.

options.text: That prayer changes God's unchanging plans by force.
options.note: The ground is the one mediator, not leverage over God.

options.text: That God is indifferent to who is saved.
options.note: God wants everyone to be saved and to know the truth.

quiz.q: What is a woman's true adornment, according to Paul?

options.text: Modesty, self-control, and good deeds fitting for those who worship God.
options.note: Verses 9 and 10 locate adornment in character and good works.

options.text: The most expensive clothing and jewelry available.
options.note: Paul contrasts good deeds with gold, pearls, and costly attire.

options.text: Complete withdrawal from all public life.
options.note: The point is godly conduct in worship, not withdrawal.

options.text: Silence born of having nothing to offer.
options.note: Women profess to worship God and are called to good works, not treated as worthless.

quiz.q: How does the study fairly present the debate over verses 11 and 12?

options.text: As a genuine disagreement among orthodox Christians over the scope of the instruction.
options.note: The study names both a creational-order reading and a situational reading, each held by faithful believers.

options.text: As proof that the Bible devalues women.
options.note: Both readings uphold the full dignity and gifting of women; this conclusion misreads the text.

options.text: As a settled matter with no legitimate discussion.
options.note: The passage is genuinely debated among those who honor Scripture.

options.text: As a passage Christians should simply ignore.
options.note: The task is to weigh it carefully, not to ignore it.

quiz.q: What grounds does Paul give in verses 13 and 14 for his instruction?

options.text: The creation order and the account of the fall in Genesis.
options.note: Adam formed first, and Eve deceived, are drawn from Genesis.

options.text: The customs of Roman law courts.
options.note: Paul appeals to Genesis, not to Roman civil custom.

options.text: A vote taken by the Ephesian elders.
options.note: His reasoning is from Scripture, not a church vote.

options.text: His personal dislike of women teachers.
options.note: He grounds it in creation and the fall, not personal preference.

questions: Paul makes prayer for everyone, including rulers we may dislike, the first priority. Who in authority do you find hardest to pray for, and will you begin to?
There is one mediator between God and men. How does resting on Christ alone free you from trying to reach God on your own terms?
Christ gave Himself a ransom for all. What captivity in your life do you most need to know He has paid to release you from?
Paul locates true adornment in good deeds and self-control rather than display. Where are you tempted to invest in outward image over inward character?
Faithful Christians read the instruction on women differently. How can you hold your own conviction on this with both firmness and humility toward those who differ?

translationNotes.note: The BSB footnote notes that woman may be rendered wife, and again in verse 12, one reason the passage is debated.
Exercise authority renders authenteo, a rare word found only here in the New Testament; the footnote also offers over her husband for over a man.
The BSB footnote gives the literal singular, She, however, will be saved, and childbearing carries the definite article, which some link to the birth of Christ.
